INDEPENDENT ADOPTION — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Riley Lee

DECLARATION OF PURPOSE — INDEPENDENT ADOPTION INFORMATION SHEET
This Independent Adoption — Information Sheet describes California's statutory process for Jordan Lee to adopt Riley Lee (born April 3, 2019), a child whom Casey Morgan, the child's birth parent, proposes to place for adoption directly with Jordan Lee rather than through a licensed adoption agency, under California Family Code Division 13, Part 2, Chapter 3 (Independent Adoptions, §§ 8800–8823). It is prepared for use alongside an actual independent adoption request contemplated for filing in the California superior court for Sacramento County.

An independent adoption is its own distinct statutory track — separate from an agency adoption, in which the State Department of Social Services, a county adoption agency, or a licensed adoption agency is a party to or joins in the adoption petition, and separate from a stepparent adoption under Family Code Chapter 5 (§§ 9000–9007), which applies only where the person adopting is the spouse or domestic partner of the child's existing legal parent. In an independent adoption, Casey Morgan personally selects Jordan Lee as the prospective adoptive parent, and a state or county agency investigates the proposed adoption and reports to the court, but is not itself a party filing or joining in the adoption petition.

This information sheet is not itself a court filing. Completing it does not adopt Riley Lee, does not terminate any parent's rights, does not accept or record any consent to adoption, and does not determine that any specific adoption should or will be granted. Only a final court decree of adoption, entered after the statutory adoption request, consent, investigation, and hearing process described in this document's companion clauses, can actually do that.

WHAT MAKES AN ADOPTION "INDEPENDENT," AS DISTINCT FROM AN AGENCY ADOPTION
California's adoption statutes define two structurally different tracks by reference to who is a party to the adoption petition, not by reference to who investigates it. Family Code § 8524 defines "independent adoption" to mean "the adoption of a child in which neither the department, county adoption agency, nor agency licensed by the department is a party to, or joins in, the adoption petition." By contrast, Family Code § 8506 defines "agency adoption" to mean "the adoption of a minor, other than an intercountry adoption, in which the department, county adoption agency, or licensed adoption agency is a party to, or joins in, the adoption petition." The distinction these two definitions draw is precise: in both an independent adoption and an agency adoption, a state or county agency has a statutory role — an independent adoption is not an unsupervised private arrangement — but only in an agency adoption is that agency itself a party to, or joiner in, the petition asking the court to grant the adoption. "The department," as referenced in both definitions, is defined by Family Code § 8518 to mean the State Department of Social Services.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "“Independent adoption” means the adoption of a child in which neither the department, county adoption agency, nor agency licensed by the department is a party to, or joins in, the adoption petition."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 8524 (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 8524 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=8524.)
  "“Agency adoption” means the adoption of a minor, other than an intercountry adoption, in which the department, county adoption agency, or licensed adoption agency is a party to, or joins in, the adoption petition."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 8506 (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 8506 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=8506.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how California law itself distinguishes an independent adoption from an agency adoption — not a claim about which state's law would govern any specific adoption, and not a claim that the adoption described in this document has been, or will be, classified by any court as an independent adoption. Family Code § 8524 and § 8506 are separate, independently numbered sections within the same Part 1 definitions chapter, and are treated here as two independent sources; § 8518's definition of "the department" is referenced for context but is not independently load-bearing for the independent/agency distinction itself, so it is not counted as a third independent source for that specific point. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine that the child or the prospective adoptive parent named in this document's companion clauses is, or is not, the subject of an independent adoption within the meaning of § 8524, and it does not file, join in, or accept any adoption petition.

BIRTH-PARENT SELECTION OF THE PROSPECTIVE ADOPTIVE PARENT, AND WHO MAY FILE THE ADOPTION REQUEST
Two separate statutory rules together give an independent adoption its defining, agency-free character at the front end. First, Family Code § 8801(a) requires that "the selection of a prospective adoptive parent or parents shall be personally made by the child's birth parent or parents and may not be delegated to an agent," and that this selection "shall be based upon personal knowledge of the prospective adoptive parent or parents" — meaning Casey Morgan, not an agency, is the one who chooses Jordan Lee as the prospective adoptive parent. Second, once a prospective adoptive parent has been so selected, Family Code § 8802(a) identifies which adult persons may then file the adoption request with the court, "in a county authorized by Section 8609.5," including, among other listed categories, "a person with whom a child has been placed for adoption," a case in which "a copy of the independent adoption placement agreement shall be attached to the petition."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "The selection of a prospective adoptive parent or parents shall be personally made by the child’s birth parent or parents and may not be delegated to an agent. The act of selection by the birth parent or parents shall be based upon personal knowledge of the prospective adoptive parent or parents."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 8801(a) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 8801(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=8801.)
  "Any of the following adult persons who desire to adopt a child may, for that purpose, file an adoption request in a county authorized by Section 8609.5: ... (3) A person with whom a child has been placed for adoption, in which case a copy of the independent adoption placement agreement shall be attached to the petition."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 8802(a) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 8802(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=8802.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of who selects the prospective adoptive parent and who may file the adoption request in a California independent adoption — not a claim about which state's law would govern any specific adoption, and not a claim that the birth parent named in this document's companion clauses has made, or the petitioner named there is eligible to make, any specific selection or filing described in this clause. Family Code § 8801 and § 8802 are separate, independently numbered sections, cited here as two independent sources; only subdivision (a) of each is quoted, and this clause does not detail § 8801(b)'s further definition of "personal knowledge," the five other filing categories listed in § 8802(a)(1)–(2) and (4)–(6), or § 8802(b)–(g)'s separate procedural requirements for the adoption request's contents and the court clerk's notice to the department. This document is informational only: it does not itself select any prospective adoptive parent, does not file any adoption request, and does not determine that the adoption described in this document's companion clauses meets these statutory requirements in any specific case.

THE REQUIRED INVESTIGATION AND REPORT BEFORE THE COURT RULES ON THE PETITION
Even though no agency is a party to the petition in an independent adoption, a state or county agency must still investigate the proposed adoption and report to the court before the adoption can be finalized. Family Code § 8806 directs that "the department or delegated county adoption agency shall accept the consent of the birth parents to the adoption of the child by the petitioners and, before filing its report with the court, shall ascertain whether the child is a proper subject for adoption and whether the proposed home is suitable for the child." Family Code § 8807(a) sets a deadline for that investigation: "[e]xcept as provided in subdivisions (b) and (c), within 180 days after receiving 50 percent of the fee, the department or delegated county adoption agency shall investigate the proposed independent adoption and, after the remaining balance of the fee is paid, submit to the court a full report of the facts disclosed by its inquiry with a recommendation regarding the granting of the petition."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "The department or delegated county adoption agency shall accept the consent of the birth parents to the adoption of the child by the petitioners and, before filing its report with the court, shall ascertain whether the child is a proper subject for adoption and whether the proposed home is suitable for the child."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 8806 (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 8806 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=8806.)
  "Except as provided in subdivisions (b) and (c), within 180 days after receiving 50 percent of the fee, the department or delegated county adoption agency shall investigate the proposed independent adoption and, after the remaining balance of the fee is paid, submit to the court a full report of the facts disclosed by its inquiry with a recommendation regarding the granting of the petition."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 8807(a) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 8807(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=8807.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the pre-decision investigation and reporting duty imposed on the department or a delegated county adoption agency in a California independent adoption — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific adoption, or about what investigation, if any, another state's process requires. Family Code § 8806 and § 8807 are separate, independently numbered sections, cited here as two independent sources; § 8807 is itself subdivided, and this clause quotes only subdivision (a) — it does not detail § 8807(b)'s rule requiring immediate filing where the investigation finds a serious question about suitability, care, or consent, § 8807(c)'s allowance for a court-granted extension of the 180-day period, or § 8807(d)'s separate rule for a petitioner residing outside California. This document does not detail the separate investigation fee structure set by Family Code § 8810, referenced in § 8807(a) but not independently verified for this document. This document is informational only: it does not itself investigate, report on, or determine the suitability of the petitioner or the home described in this document's companion clauses, and it does not determine whether, or by when, any such investigation and report will occur in any specific case.

HOW AND BEFORE WHOM CONSENT TO AN INDEPENDENT ADOPTION IS SIGNED
California law requires a birth parent's consent to an independent adoption to be signed under agency supervision, not merely in a private agreement between the birth parent and the prospective adoptive parent. Family Code § 8814(a) provides that, except in a narrow circumstance described in Family Code § 7662, "the consent of the birth parent or parents who did not place the child for adoption, as described in Section 8801.3, to the adoption shall be signed in the presence of an agent of the department or of a delegated county adoption agency on a form prescribed by the department," and that "[t]he consent shall be filed with the clerk of the appropriate superior court."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "Except as provided in Section 7662, the consent of the birth parent or parents who did not place the child for adoption, as described in Section 8801.3, to the adoption shall be signed in the presence of an agent of the department or of a delegated county adoption agency on a form prescribed by the department. The consent shall be filed with the clerk of the appropriate superior court."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 8814(a) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 8814(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=8814.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the procedure California law requires for signing consent to an independent adoption — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific adoption, or about what consent procedure, if any, another state's process requires, and not a claim that the birth parent named in this document's companion clauses has signed, or is required to sign, consent in any specific manner in any specific case. Family Code § 8814 is not subdivided into independent sources for purposes of this clause: only subdivision (a) is quoted, and no additional, separately numbered statutory section was located and independently confirmed for this specific procedural point, so this clause rests on a single statutory section. This clause does not detail § 8814(b)'s rule on the evidentiary effect of a consent reciting sole custody, § 8814(c)'s separate procedure for a birth parent located outside California, § 8814(d)'s rule preserving a minor birth parent's right to consent, or the cross-referenced exception in Family Code § 7662, none of which were independently verified for this document. This document is informational only: it does not itself take, witness, or file any consent to adoption, and it does not determine that any signature described in this document's companion clauses satisfies this statutory procedure.

THE 30-DAY RIGHT TO REVOKE CONSENT, AND WHEN CONSENT BECOMES PERMANENT
California law gives a birth parent who has signed consent to an independent adoption a specific, time-limited window to change that decision before it becomes final. Family Code § 8814.5(a) provides that "[a]fter a consent to the adoption is signed by the birth parent or parents pursuant to Section 8801.3 or 8814, the birth parent or parents signing the consent shall have 30 days to take one of the following actions," including, under paragraph (a)(1), to "[s]ign and deliver to the department or delegated county adoption agency a written statement revoking the consent and requesting the child to be returned to the birth parent or parents." Absent an earlier signed waiver of the right to revoke, paragraph (a)(3) provides that the birth parent may instead "[a]llow the consent to become a permanent consent on the 31st day after signing," and subdivision (b) confirms that "[t]he consent may not be revoked after a waiver of the right to revoke consent has been signed or after 30 days, beginning on the date the consent was signed ... whichever occurs first." A separate section describes the practical consequence of this timing: Family Code § 8815(a) provides that "[o]nce the revocable consent to adoption has become permanent as provided in Section 8814.5, the consent to the adoption by the prospective adoptive parents may not be withdrawn," while § 8815(b) provides that "[b]efore the time when the revocable consent becomes permanent as provided in Section 8814.5, the birth parent or parents may request return of the child," in which case "the child shall immediately be returned to the requesting birth parent or parents, unless a court orders otherwise."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "After a consent to the adoption is signed by the birth parent or parents pursuant to Section 8801.3 or 8814, the birth parent or parents signing the consent shall have 30 days to take one of the following actions: (1) Sign and deliver to the department or delegated county adoption agency a written statement revoking the consent and requesting the child to be returned to the birth parent or parents. ... (3) Allow the consent to become a permanent consent on the 31st day after signing. (b) The consent may not be revoked after a waiver of the right to revoke consent has been signed or after 30 days, beginning on the date the consent was signed or as provided in paragraph (1) of subdivision (a), whichever occurs first."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 8814.5(a), (a)(1), (a)(3) & (b) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 8814.5(a)-(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=8814.5.)
  "(a) Once the revocable consent to adoption has become permanent as provided in Section 8814.5, the consent to the adoption by the prospective adoptive parents may not be withdrawn. (b) Before the time when the revocable consent becomes permanent as provided in Section 8814.5, the birth parent or parents may request return of the child. In that case the child shall immediately be returned to the requesting birth parent or parents, unless a court orders otherwise."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 8815(a) & (b) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 8815(a)-(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=8815.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the specific 30-day consent-revocation window and permanence rule California law applies to an independent adoption — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific adoption, or about what revocation period, if any, another state's process allows, and not a claim that any consent described in this document's companion clauses has been, will be, revoked, waived, or made permanent in any specific case. Within Family Code § 8814.5, subdivisions (a)(1), (a)(3), and (b) are subsections of the same statutory section and are treated here as one source, not as separate independent sources for one another; Family Code § 8815 is a separate, independently numbered section, and its subdivisions (a) and (b) are likewise treated as one source internal to that section. Taken together, § 8814.5 and § 8815 are counted here as two independent statutory sources for the revocability rule generally, though neither corroborates the other's specific 30-day figure, which appears only in § 8814.5. This clause does not detail § 8814.5(a)(2)'s separate procedure for signing an earlier waiver of the right to revoke, which can shorten this window, or § 8815(c)'s separate provision on reporting fitness concerns to a child welfare agency, neither of which is independently verified here beyond the text quoted. This document is informational only: it does not itself calculate whether any specific 30-day period has run, does not revoke, waive, or accept any consent, and does not determine whether any child described in this document's companion clauses must be returned to, or may be retained by, any party in any specific case.

HOW AN INDEPENDENT ADOPTION DIFFERS, STRUCTURALLY, FROM A STEPPARENT ADOPTION
California law places independent adoptions and stepparent adoptions in separate chapters of the same statutory part, built around a different eligibility premise. Family Code § 8524 defines "independent adoption" as "the adoption of a child in which neither the department, county adoption agency, nor agency licensed by the department is a party to, or joins in, the adoption petition" — a definition that says nothing about the adopting person's relationship to the child's existing legal parent, because none is required. By contrast, Family Code § 9000(a), in the separate Chapter 5 governing stepparent adoptions, authorizes only "[a] stepparent desiring to adopt a child of the stepparent's spouse" to "file a petition in any county authorized by Section 8609.5" (with § 9000(b) extending the same right to a domestic partner adopting the other partner's child). An independent adoption under Chapter 3 (§§ 8800–8823) is available to a wider, differently defined set of prospective adoptive parents identified in Family Code § 8802(a) — including certain relatives, a person named in a deceased parent's will, a person with whom the child has already been placed for adoption, and certain long-term legal guardians — none of which requires the petitioner to be the spouse or domestic partner of the child's existing legal parent, and none of which is satisfied merely because the petitioner is a stepparent.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "“Independent adoption” means the adoption of a child in which neither the department, county adoption agency, nor agency licensed by the department is a party to, or joins in, the adoption petition."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 8524 (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 8524 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=8524.)
  "A stepparent desiring to adopt a child of the stepparent’s spouse may for that purpose file a petition in any county authorized by Section 8609.5."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 9000(a) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 9000(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=9000.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that California places independent adoptions and stepparent adoptions in separate statutory chapters with different eligibility premises — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific adoption, and not a claim that the adoption described in this document's companion clauses is, or is not, eligible for either track; that depends on the specific relationship between the prospective adoptive parent and the child's existing legal parent, among other facts. Family Code § 8524 and § 9000(a) are separate, independently numbered sections in different chapters, cited here as two independent sources; § 8802(a) is referenced for the breadth of the independent-adoption filing categories but is the same section already cited and detailed in this document's companion clause on birth-parent selection and filing, so it is not counted as an additional independent source here. This clause does not restate every eligibility category listed in § 8802(a) or § 9000(a)–(g)'s further procedural rules, and it does not address the possibility that a specific individual could, on different facts, qualify under either chapter (for example, as both a relative and a stepparent) — which chapter in fact governs a specific petition is a determination for the filing court, not this document. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine which statutory chapter governs the adoption described in this document's companion clauses, and it does not file, join in, or grant any adoption petition.

expectedJSON.body: California law gives a birth parent who has signed consent to an independent adoption a specific, time-limited window to change that decision before it becomes final. Family Code § 8814.5(a) provides that "[a]fter a consent to the adoption is signed by the birth parent or parents pursuant to Section 8801.3 or 8814, the birth parent or parents signing the consent shall have 30 days to take one of the following actions," including, under paragraph (a)(1), to "[s]ign and deliver to the department or delegated county adoption agency a written statement revoking the consent and requesting the child to be returned to the birth parent or parents." Absent an earlier signed waiver of the right to revoke, paragraph (a)(3) provides that the birth parent may instead "[a]llow the consent to become a permanent consent on the 31st day after signing," and subdivision (b) confirms that "[t]he consent may not be revoked after a waiver of the right to revoke consent has been signed or after 30 days, beginning on the date the consent was signed ... whichever occurs first." A separate section describes the practical consequence of this timing: Family Code § 8815(a) provides that "[o]nce the revocable consent to adoption has become permanent as provided in Section 8814.5, the consent to the adoption by the prospective adoptive parents may not be withdrawn," while § 8815(b) provides that "[b]efore the time when the revocable consent becomes permanent as provided in Section 8814.5, the birth parent or parents may request return of the child," in which case "the child shall immediately be returned to the requesting birth parent or parents, unless a court orders otherwise."

expectedJSON.body: California law places independent adoptions and stepparent adoptions in separate chapters of the same statutory part, built around a different eligibility premise. Family Code § 8524 defines "independent adoption" as "the adoption of a child in which neither the department, county adoption agency, nor agency licensed by the department is a party to, or joins in, the adoption petition" — a definition that says nothing about the adopting person's relationship to the child's existing legal parent, because none is required. By contrast, Family Code § 9000(a), in the separate Chapter 5 governing stepparent adoptions, authorizes only "[a] stepparent desiring to adopt a child of the stepparent's spouse" to "file a petition in any county authorized by Section 8609.5" (with § 9000(b) extending the same right to a domestic partner adopting the other partner's child). An independent adoption under Chapter 3 (§§ 8800–8823) is available to a wider, differently defined set of prospective adoptive parents identified in Family Code § 8802(a) — including certain relatives, a person named in a deceased parent's will, a person with whom the child has already been placed for adoption, and certain long-term legal guardians — none of which requires the petitioner to be the spouse or domestic partner of the child's existing legal parent, and none of which is satisfied merely because the petitioner is a stepparent.
